The flyer transcript contains `RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE`, but `Riverton`
matches two places in the reference table. The coordinator needs both
possibilities to remain visible.

A map needs coordinates, not only a place name. The team can join a mention to a
small reference file, then keep the unresolved cases visible.

::: {.callout-note}
The places, lab, and flyer here belong to an invented Riverton setting.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain geocoding and gazetteers in plain language.
- join place mentions to latitude and longitude.
- detect duplicate place-name matches.
- return a miss when a place is absent.
- explain why context matters in geocoding.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load the offline reference files

**Geocoding** links a place name in text to coordinates, the latitude and
longitude that locate a point on a map. CSV files supply examples, while dplyr
and tibble prepare tables. digest calculates a file fingerprint, a code that
the lesson compares with the expected fingerprint.

A **gazetteer** lists place names and their locations. Gazetteers may be public,
open-licence, or commercial reference datasets. This invented local gazetteer
lets the lesson execute offline.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(digest)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

gazetteer <- read_csv(
  "data/riverton/riverton-gazetteer.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    place_name = col_character(),
    place_type = col_character(),
    latitude = col_double(),
    longitude = col_double(),
    parent = col_character()
  )
)

metadata <- read_csv(
  "data/riverton/riverton-reference-metadata.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    artifact = col_character(),
    description = col_character(),
    source = col_character(),
    license = col_character(),
    created_on = col_character(),
    fingerprint = col_character()
  )
)

gazetteer_hash <- digest(
  paste(read_lines("data/riverton/riverton-gazetteer.csv"), collapse = "\n"),
  algo = "sha256",
  serialize = FALSE
)
expected_hash <- metadata |>
  filter(artifact == "riverton-gazetteer.csv") |>
  pull(fingerprint)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  gazetteer,
  col.names = c("Place name", "Type", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Parent"),
  caption = "Invented Riverton gazetteer used offline",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(c("readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "digest") %in% loadedNamespaces()))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(nrow(gazetteer), 9L),
  identical(sum(gazetteer$place_name == "Riverton"), 2L),
  identical(gazetteer_hash, expected_hash)
)
```

The reference table has nine rows. The duplicate `Riverton` rows are deliberate:
one is in Marrow County, Calder, and one is in Tidewater. The `parent` column
names the larger place that contains a row. The coordinates are arbitrary teaching
points, not the locations of real sites.

This table classifies `Riverton Skills Centre` as a building. The
entity-linking lesson uses the same name for an organisation. The same string
can denote either a place or an organisation. Named-entity systems must account
for this ORG-versus-place ambiguity.

## Join mentions to the gazetteer

The team starts with five manually selected place mentions. One comes from the
Riverton flyer text. Four are constructed checks written in the same setting so
we can see resolved, ambiguous, and not-found cases together.

```{r}
place_mentions <- bind_rows(
  sentences |>
    filter(sentence_id == "s023") |>
    transmute(
      mention_id = sentence_id,
      source = "Riverton text",
      text,
      mention = "Riverton"
    ),
  tibble(
    mention_id = c("place-02", "place-03", "place-04", "place-05"),
    source = "constructed check",
    text = c(
      "Evening classes at Riverton Skills Centre",
      "Applicants in Riverton can apply by October 15",
      "Weekend shifts serve Bellhaven",
      "The route reaches West Calder"
    ),
    mention = c("Riverton Skills Centre", "Riverton", "Bellhaven", "West Calder")
  )
)

geocoded_rows <- place_mentions |>
  left_join(
    gazetteer,
    by = join_by(mention == place_name),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  geocoded_rows,
  col.names = c(
    "Mention ID", "Source", "Text", "Mention", "Type",
    "Latitude", "Longitude", "Parent"
  ),
  caption = "Joining place mentions to the gazetteer",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(place_mentions), 5L),
  identical(nrow(geocoded_rows), 7L),
  identical(sum(is.na(geocoded_rows$latitude)), 1L)
)
```

The `relationship` argument tells dplyr that one mention may match several rows.
The code explicitly permits these multiple matches to preserve ambiguity. The
join returns seven rows from five mentions because `Riverton` matches twice.
`West Calder` receives no coordinates because it is not in the gazetteer.

## Name the unresolved states

A geocoder must report unresolved mentions. The next table gives
each mention a status.

```{r}
mention_status <- geocoded_rows |>
  summarise(
    matches = sum(!is.na(latitude)),
    candidate_parents = paste(na.omit(parent), collapse = ", "),
    .by = c(mention_id, source, text, mention)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    candidate_parents = if_else(candidate_parents == "", "none", candidate_parents),
    status = case_when(
      matches == 0L ~ "not found",
      matches > 1L ~ "ambiguous",
      TRUE ~ "resolved"
    )
  )

status_counts <- tibble(status = c("resolved", "ambiguous", "not found")) |>
  left_join(
    mention_status |>
      count(status, name = "mentions"),
    by = join_by(status)
  ) |>
  mutate(mentions = coalesce(mentions, 0L))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  mention_status,
  col.names = c(
    "Mention ID", "Source", "Text", "Mention", "Matches",
    "Candidate parents", "Status"
  ),
  caption = "Each mention receives a geocoding status",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  status_counts,
  col.names = c("Status", "Mentions"),
  caption = "Resolved, ambiguous, and not-found mentions",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(status_counts$mentions, c(2L, 2L, 1L)),
  identical(sum(status_counts$mentions), 5L)
)
```

Two mentions resolve to one row. Two are ambiguous. One is not found. These
counts describe only the five mentions in this lesson.

## Add context when the name is not enough

The name `Riverton` alone does not distinguish the two rows. The flyer gives
no county, so the analyst supplies the context below to demonstrate the rule.
A pipeline needs that value from a document header, posting address, or stated
collection scope.

```{r}
riverton_candidates <- geocoded_rows |>
  filter(mention_id == "s023") |>
  select(mention, latitude, longitude, parent)

supplied_context <- tibble(
  mention = "Riverton",
  parent_context = "Marrow County"
)

with_parent_context <- riverton_candidates |>
  inner_join(supplied_context, by = join_by(mention)) |>
  filter(parent == parent_context)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  riverton_candidates,
  col.names = c("Mention", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Parent"),
  caption = "The name Riverton has two candidate locations",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  with_parent_context,
  col.names = c("Mention", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Parent", "Context supplied"),
  caption = "Parent context narrows the candidate list",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(riverton_candidates), 2L),
  identical(nrow(with_parent_context), 1L),
  identical(with_parent_context$latitude, 41.821)
)
```

The context row shows a decision rule, not evidence from the flyer. Without the
parent region, a prior belief, or surrounding text, the two `Riverton` rows remain
equally possible.

## Geocoding in production

This local exact-match join demonstrates geocoding. Production systems use
specialized APIs, such as OpenStreetMap/Nominatim, rather than raw string joins.
Packages such as `tidygeocoder` in R or `geopy` in Python provide interfaces
to those services.

When using a live service, several boundaries and limits apply:
- **Match precision**: APIs can use fuzzy matching to compare similar names rather than require identical strings. Examine geocoding results with low confidence scores.
- **Service boundaries**: Rate limits and Terms of Service often dictate how many requests you can make.
- **Caching**: Locally stored results prevent redundant network calls and reduce processing time.
- **Privacy and re-identification**: Text sent to an external API can reveal personal locations. A self-hosted geocoder, such as a local Nominatim instance, keeps that text on your infrastructure.

## What to remember

- A gazetteer is a reference list of place names with locations attached.
- Geocoding turns a place mention into coordinates.
- Joining by name can return more than one coordinate pair.
- A miss should stay a miss rather than becoming a guess.
- Context such as a parent region can reduce the candidate list.
- `ambiguous` and `not found` are valid geocoding results.

This teaching gazetteer can map `Riverton Skills Centre` and `Bellhaven`. The
word `Riverton` still has two candidate locations, and `West Calder` has none.
